issue_context.title: Filesystem resize is required after snapshot restore / volume clone
issue_context.body:
Kubernetes should resize filesystem on a volume when it's created as a clone of a smaller volume / smaller snapshot is restored into it.

Example:
1. User takes a snapshot of 1 GiB volume with ext3 filesystem on it.
2. User restores the snapshot into 2 GiB volume.
    2.1 CSI driver restores the snapshot into a bigger volume, but ext3 filesystem still uses only 1 GiB of space.
3. CSI driver should make sure that the filesystem on the volume has been resized before the volume is mounted into a pod.

There are few steps needed:

* [x] Clarify behavior of `CreateVolume` CSI call, https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/pull/452
* [ ] Update CSI drivers to the new behavior.
  * [x] Move filesystem resize code from kubernetes/kuberenetes to kubernetes/mount-utils, so all CSI drivers can re-use the same code https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/99039 
  * [x] Enhance the code above to compare the volume size from block device perspective and from filesystem perspective. See https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-ebs-csi-driver/pull/595 for proof of concept. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/99042
  * [ ] File issues in all community CSI drivers that we care about & fix them.
* [ ] Update csi-tests to (optionally?) check for volume size when cloning / restoring snapshot to a bigger size. https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/csi-test/issues/325
comments:
/assign
/sig storage
/priority important-soon
True, considering the CSI spec allows restore to a bigger size volume, we should have the support from CO.

> * Update the external-provisioner to create PVs that are marked for resize when a volume clone / snapshot restore is bigger than the original.

This is hard, Kubernets PV controller overwrites `PVC.Status.Capacity` on binding. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8422044f1746354393ea5b617e2bde5c24c0f829/pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller.go#L771-L784

Therefore the external-provisioner cannot create PVC as "marked for resize on node", i.e. with `PVC.Spec.Capacity` = `PV.Spec.Capacity` = the real size of the new volume) and with `PVC.Status.Capacity` = size of the original volume.

We either need to change the binding mechanism not to overwrite `PVC.Status.Size` or add a flag (annotation?) that marks the volume for resize on node, even when `PVC.Spec.Capacity == PVC.Status.Capacity`.

Talked to @gnufied:

* The external-provisioner could mark `PVC.Status` for resize on node:
  * Set `PVC.Status.Capacity` to the original volume size.
  * Add `FileSystemResizePending` condition to the PVC.
  * As result, the extenal-provisioner needs to modify `PVC.Status`, which needs new RBAC and is a breaking change.
* The PV controller could respect `PVC.Status.Capacity`, if set.

We discussed and rejected adding a new flag / annotation to PV by the external-provisioner for kubelet to call NodeExpandVolume on the first mount. Such a flag would need to be cleared by  kubelet and kubelet can't modify PVs.

From latest discussion last week, I believe the conclusion was to have external-provisioner set `PV.Spec.Capacity` to the smaller size. Then we just let the rest of the normal resize flow continue. No need to have provisioner set the conditions.

@kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs

@msau42 we agreed to set conditions too because we want to be as close as possible to external-resizer. If there is some tooling that depends on condition for resizing pending on node, we don't want to break any such tooling. currently kubelet does not depend on condition for node expansion though.
Why can't we let resize controller set the condition when it sees pvc size != pv size?
@msau42 hmm good point. I think that should work but we may have to verify that flow.
I think we can do that, but only with a change to the CSI spec wording, because the current implication is that should not be necessary.

review_comments: same as before. We need unit tests for the parsing logic.
nit: please add a test with unknown FS
We should write unit tests for all this parsing logic.

Why not just use statfs to get the size of /any/ filesystem, instead of hard-coding and scraping individual filesystem utilities? statfs is the generic interface to query the kernel about the size of a mounted filesystem.

See statfs(2) and the -f option in statfs(1)
Hm, well, this doesn't count the log blocks I guess. Not sure what your threshold for "should try to grow" is.

Or even just:
# df -B1 --output=size /boot
 1B-blocks
1063256064

and again this ignores space consumed by journals or other internal fs housekeeping, but it may be better to use standard APIs like statfs(2) (which is how df gets its information)

@sandeen, I may miss something here, but IMO `statfs` shows size of the filesystem available for actual files (i.e. without journal and other FS metadata), while xfs_info shows the actual size occupied by the filesystem on a device, incl. journal, inodes, and whatnot.

We need to reliably check if we should call `resize2fs` / `xfs_growfs`, i.e. there is some extra space on the device that the filesystem does not know about.

```
$ df  --output=size /boot
1K-blocks
   999320
$ dumpe2fs /dev/nvme0n1p2
Block count:              262144
Block size:               4096
```
999320 * 1024 = 1023303680
262144 * 4096 = 1073741824

That's quite a difference.

It's < 5%, or about 58MB.

So, yes - as I mentioned it won't count filesystem overhead like the journal, or inode tables & bitmaps on ext4.

What is your typical image size, roughly?

On a 2G filesystem image, with default mkfs, filesystem overhead is about 5% for ext4, and < 1% for xfs.  If that is "quite a difference" and outside your threshold, then you may be stuck with the more fragile screenscraping as proposed.

Or, you could  just do:

```
mount
stat -f
if device is more than 10% bigger than free blocks
    try resize2fs/xfs_growfs
    # if you guessed wrong, the resize will be a no-op.
```
Or, just try a growfs after each initial mount, which is going to be quick and harmless if the filesystem is already maximally sized.

That way you could dispense with the screenscraping, which has a reasonable chance of breaking in the future, because admin tool text output is really not an API, and unfortunately there is not any real API to tell you exactly what the last block known to a filesystem is.

> just try a growfs after each initial mount, which is going to be quick and harmless if the filesystem is already maximally sized.

How safe is this for xfs and ext3/ext4? Since we will do it with every mount() and containers can move around the cluster rather quickly, we need it to be fast enough (say same as mount()?) and reliable (won't ever harm the FS, even when it gets SIGINT).

> What is your typical image size, roughly?

It starts with 1 GB and goes to hundreds of GB. But I am not sure it's relevant. If user extends the volume by 1% (which can be say 1GB), we'd like the volume to be be expanded.
Let's chat on IRC when you get a chance, higher bandwidth than github comments might help.

summary of conversation on IRC, here are the options:
```
<sandeen> 1) use df, and accept a small % error
<sandeen> 2) scrape filesystem utilities and hope they don't change 
<sandeen> 3) always call resize, which would be a no-op if already maximally sized
<sandeen> 4) use filesystem-specific but more well-defined APIs where they exist
<sandeen> ...
<sandeen> 5) wait for a common kernel solution :(
```

We'd prefer 4) if available and for xfs we were able to find `xfs_io -c statfs <mount>` , which is much easier to parse. In addition, it uses [`ioctl` to get the geometry](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/ioctl_xfs_fsgeometry.2.html). @AndyXiangLi can you try `ioctl` with some interface to make unit testing possible?

There is no ioctl for ext3/4, so 2) is IMO the best option and luckily `dumpe2fs` is not that horrible to parse.
Correction: is go & `ioctl` portable to ARM / PPC / s390x and other weird architectures that Kubernetes supports? If not, do not hesitate to fall back to parsing `xfs_io -c statfs`.

If you parse the xfs_io output, the field you want is "geom.datablocks" to get the actual, complete number of all blocks on the filesytem's data device. Note that this is only available when running the xfs_io "statfs" command on an xfs filesystem, non-xfs filesystems will only return the basic statfs(2) information, same as df.
We should ensure that if provided filesystem is something we don't know how to parse, proper error and message is returned back to the caller.
